statements.body: The ramen shop currently loses money by over-ordering perishables and running out of staples.
Ordering decisions are currently made by gut feel rather than data.
Supplier invoices will be a primary data input to the system.
A nightly stock count will be a primary data input to the system.
The system will combine inventory tracking and budget tracking in a single tool.
Replacing gut-feel ordering with data-driven decisions will meaningfully reduce waste and stockout costs.
Who performs the nightly stock count and enters it into the system?
How are supplier invoices currently received and in what format (paper, email, PDF, EDI)?
How many distinct SKUs or ingredients does the shop track?
What is the target budget period — daily, weekly, monthly — for the budget tracker?

concerns.coverage: The shop over-orders perishables and runs out of staples because ordering is driven by gut feel; the direct cost is wasted spend and lost sales from stockouts.
The operator is a ramen shop (single location implied); the idea does not name who will use the system day-to-day — owner, manager, or kitchen staff — nor how many people that involves.
Invoices from suppliers and a nightly stock count are the two entry points; the idea implies ordering decisions are the exit point, but intermediate steps and handoffs are not described.
Supplier invoices and nightly stock-count figures are the core data; format, volume, and retention requirements are not stated.
No budget, timeline, stack, or compliance constraints are stated; single-location ramen shop implies small team and likely limited technical resources.
Success is implied when ordering decisions come from numbers rather than gut feel, reducing over-ordering and stockouts, but no measurable threshold or observation method is specified.

candidates.body: Who will use the system day to day — the owner, a manager, or kitchen staff — and does that person also perform and enter the nightly stock count?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger flags that no operator is named; an unowned nightly count is the single biggest risk to the whole data pipeline, since a count that nobody reliably does starves both trackers. Answering this bounds the first slice around a real person's routine and capture context.

candidates.body: In what format do supplier invoices arrive today — paper, email, PDF, or electronic feed?
candidates.whySelected: Invoices are one of only two data inputs, and their format determines whether the first slice needs manual entry, OCR, or file parsing — a decision that dominates early build cost for a small shop.

candidates.body: What single number would tell you the system is working after the first month — for example, dollars of spoiled stock discarded per week or count of stockout incidents?
candidates.whySelected: Success coverage notes no measurable threshold exists; picking one observable metric makes the waste-reduction hypothesis testable and tells the first slice which data it must capture from day one.

candidates.body: Roughly how many distinct ingredients or SKUs does the shop stock, and how many of those are perishable?
candidates.whySelected: Volume determines whether a nightly count is a five-minute clipboard task or an operational burden that will be skipped; it directly shapes how lightweight the capture workflow must be to survive real kitchen conditions.

readyAdvice.why: All core concerns have some coverage, but the two data inputs have no named owner or format, and success has no observable metric. The first vertical slice cannot be bounded until at least the operator and invoice-format questions are answered; safety, quality, and non-goals also remain unexamined.
